Photograph: Jeremy Poland/Getty Images California California woman charged with murder after allegedly killing husband with flagpole SF Gate reports bond for Vicky Kyung Mi Kim, 65, set at $10m after man found dead at couple’s Palm Desert home Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 11 Sep 2026 20.56 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 20.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 65-year-old California woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after allegedly fatally wounding her husband with a flagpole, according to SF Gate. On 4 September, Palm Desert sheriff’s deputies responded to an “unknown trouble call” in The Enclave, a luxury condominium community. Upon arrival, officers located an individual with “traumatic injuries” that appeared to be from a physical assault and pronounced them dead. Vicky Kyung Mi Kim was taken into custody on suspicion of murder. The victim was her spouse, SF Gate reported. Her bail has been set at $10m, according to court documents. The events leading up to the deadly incident remain unknown, but court documents show Kim had a history of recent domestic violence. In January, she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of battery of a spouse or cohabitant and a misdemeanor charge of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse related to a separate violation. Kim entered a guilty plea for violating a protective order. The couple had previous arguments over finances and infidelity allegations, KESQ News Channel 3 reported . Molly Smith, a spokesperson for the Riverside county district attorney’s office, referenced Kim’s legal troubles to SF Gate: “In January of this year, our office charged Ms Kim with a felony, obtained criminal protective orders, and intended to aggressively prosecute her for her crimes against her husband.” In a statement, obtained by KESQ, Smith elaborated on Kim’s record. “Despite our office’s clear objections, a judge resolved all of the defendant’s cases as misdemeanors, released her from custody, and terminated all protective orders that prosecutors worked hard to obtain,” Smith said. The judge could not be immediately identified for comment. https://aa.com.tr/en/eurasia/russia-gran.text: World Eurasia Russia grants Serbian airlines right to operate regular flights to Kaliningrad region Russian exclave gets Serbian air service as EU airlines remain banned from Russian airspace Elena Teslova 07 September 2026 • Update : 07 September 2026 MOSCOW Serbian airlines will be allowed to operate regular flights to Russia’s Kaliningrad region after an agreement between aviation authorities of the two countries, the Russian Transport Ministry said on Monday. Under the agreement, designated Serbian carriers will receive the right to operate regular flights to Kaliningrad, the ministry said, without specifying when the services would begin or which airlines would operate them. Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, separated from mainland Russia by Lithuania and Belarus and bordered by NATO members Lithuania and Poland. Its position has made the region a focus of security tensions in the Baltic, particularly since 2022, with disputes over transit through Lithuania and increased military activity and air-policing incidents around the exclave. Serbia has remained one of the few European countries maintaining direct scheduled air links with Russia since 2022, when the EU banned Russian carriers from its airspace and Russia imposed reciprocal restrictions on EU airlines. Air Serbia continued operating flights between Belgrade and Russian cities, making Serbia an important direct air link between Russia and Europe outside the EU. The EU currently has no airlines flying to, from or over Russian airspace, while EASA continues to advise against operations in parts of western Russian airspace. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story LATEST NEWS All UN condemns continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, urges restraint Türkiye promoting COP31 presidency in New York Turkish, Vietnamese leaders gather in New York for talks Malaysia’s MIHAS 2026 halal trade showcase set to begin in Kuala Lumpur Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure could make coming winter harder for civilians Lithuania says it will not join Eurovision 2027 boycott over Israel’s participation Israel blocks Gaza patients from leaving for treatment for 2nd day over Jewish holidays See All Witkoff says ‘substantive progress’ made in US efforts to end Russia-Ukraine war Russia calls for Iran to be included in a Gulf security system

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Maricarmen’s case was taken up by Madrid’s tenants’ union in city where the right to housing is a live issue. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Maricarmen’s case was taken up by Madrid’s tenants’ union in city where the right to housing is a live issue. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock Spain Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district. Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest. Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88. View image in fullscreen Maricarmen is overwhelmed by emotion at an event organised by housing activists the day before her eviction. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office. Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms. When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner. They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored. In a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators rally against Maricarmen’s eviction in Madrid’s El Retiro neighbourhood. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock “I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.” The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment. The most beautiful act of resistance I’ve seen: Madrid tenants fighting landlords with art | Leah Pattem Read more Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.” However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.” So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain . https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/05/roma.text: Romania's head of state, Nicusor Dan, on Monday signed a law aimed at reducing the country's bear population, a bill he had previously challenged on constitutional grounds and sent back to parliament for reconsideration.The legislation, which was re-adopted by the Chamber of Deputies on 16 September, allows the preventive shooting of 859 brown bears this year. A further 110 protected large wild animals may be hunted as an intervention measure if they pose a threat to human life.In recent years it has become common in Romania for bears to appear in inhabited areas, and the number of bear attacks has risen sharply, with more and more fatal incidents.According to the results of an earlier survey mapping the brown bear population, Romania is home to Europe's largest bear population and the greatest genetic diversity among bear species.The study put the number of individuals at between 10,600 and 12,700.Last week, Covasna County prefect Ráduly István warned that, because of the limited time available, it would be impossible to meet this year's quota. He pointed out that in the Szeklerland county 86 bears should be culled this year, of which 30 have already been removed, but there is not enough time left to reach the full quota.The government's local representative said the law was much needed because both the number of bears and the damage they cause had increased significantly in the county. In the first eight months of this year, around 300 emergency calls were registered over bears straying into built-up areas and there were also two bear attacks.Time running out to tackle overpopulation?The law, initiated by the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (RMDSZ) and now revised, will enter into force once it is published in the official gazette. Some officials, however, warn that it is now impossible to fulfil this year's quota, as the months-long legal wrangle has left too little time to shoot several hundred large wild animals.Nicusor Dan sent the draft law back to parliament in August after first lodging a constitutional challenge, which was rejected by the Constitutional Court. He asked parliament to review and supplement the legislation, arguing that the previously adopted law needed clarification on several points.The Chamber of Deputies approved the bill without amendments, in the form already adopted by the Senate. During the debate some MPs urged that the law be put into practice as soon as possible.Senator Tánczos Barna, acting deputy prime minister and one of the initiators, recalled that the alliance had requested nearly a year ago that preventive quotas be doubled for this year and for 2027.He said this step followed a scientific survey which confirmed that the overpopulation of bears in Romania can only be curbed through more effective intervention, and that immediate action against dangerous bears does not replace broader population control measures.

Photograph: DITO/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Students conduct marching drills amid haze from forest and land fires at the courtyard of the Mujahidin Grand Mosque in Pontianak, West Kalimantan. Photograph: DITO/AFP/Getty Images Indonesia Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies Wed 7 Oct 2026 23.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses. The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents. ‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guide Read more None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October. “We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters. Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia , where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting. Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires. The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines. The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said. The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth. Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.” He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster. A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed. The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.
